# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

content.content:
=== F-167
- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion and keeps each example that the rule refuses, marked "Not allowed"; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. The covariance example, the empty list, the empty optional value and the root type `Object`'s algebraic supertraits each stand beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). A subtrait of every instantiation stays as the counterexample that introduces the rule, and the internal appendix's refused examples get a callout each. The checker does not yet refuse two cases: an object that extends two instantiations that differ only in a `bool` argument (row 406), and one that extends two instantiations of one trait where one instantiation's argument is the object's own static parameter, such as `O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` (row 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; its section 4.2 (the calculi's callout).
=== F-168
- F-168 **The specification's number chapters describe the flat library, and its advanced chapter on rational quantities stays word for word under a callout that marks it superseded.** The eight number types are siblings under `Number` (F-131). They convert by the library's coercions (P-74), and every other conversion is explicit, such as `asFloat(x)`. The sign-refined types, such as positive ℚ, are gone; a program tests a value's sign at run time (P-80). ℚ holds +∞, −∞ and 0/0, and claims neither a field nor a total order. `QQ` extends the four algebraic traits that the library declares on it, `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardMinMax`, `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and their laws hold for the finite rationals. F-172 gives the integer chapter's rules. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md` section 3; `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:245-250` (ℚ's traits); `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14` (the callout).
=== F-169
- F-169 **The Working Draft never wrote static-argument inference, never named the type that a library gives an integer numeral, and never named a range's integer type; the specification's text on these is the revival's.** The Working Draft's inference chapter is a heading and notes. It described numeral types, such as `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, and said that libraries define coercions from numerals to integers and rationals. But a note of its own leaves the numeral types' hierarchy undescribed, and it names no type that a library declares for a numeral. Its ranges section names no integer type. The later restart adds nothing on the three. So a citation of the specification on them cites the revival, not the team. The revised text states F-173's inference rule and F-170's ranges, and gives an integer numeral the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, its four numbers as static arguments (P-174). Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 1 and 2; `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:87-96` and `:132-148` (the note and the coercions); `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:146-161` (the callout on the numeral types).
=== F-170
- F-170 **The specification's ranges are over ℤ32, and its own ranges over wider integer types are respelled.** An integer numeral, and a `nat` or `int` parameter, used as an operand of an explicit range, such as `a` or `n` in `a#n`, converts to ℤ32 (row 485, fixed). An operand of any other integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter must have a wider integer type runs over a range of ℤ32 values and widens each element. The two examples that built `ZZ64` ranges run over ℤ32, and `ant testSpecData`, a gate step, runs both (F-114). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; `Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:42-60` and `:90-111`.
=== F-171
- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the restart's Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type.** So a trait or object that extends the closed trait must be below a listed type, with two exceptions. A trait with a `comprises` clause of its own may stay unlisted if each of its own listed types is below a listed type of the closed trait. A trait with static parameters may stay unlisted if at least one type extends it and every type that extends it is below a listed type. A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. The text does not say whether a bare type variable may be listed; walk overflows its stack on one (row 407). The compiled checker departs in three ways: it checks only the closed trait's immediate subtypes (row 487), it reads the clause in the subtrait's own type-variable names (row 489), and it finds extenders by the simple text of a name (row 490). Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic/traits.tex:246-269`.
=== F-172
- F-172 **The specification's integer chapter states the library's integer rules.** The getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` keep the value or throw `IntegerOverflow`. `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the bits and throw nothing: `narrow` converts a `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, and an `NN64` to `NN32`, by keeping the low 32 bits, so a value that does not fit wraps. `ZZ` has neither `narrow` nor `widen`. `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` work on the five integer types. On `ZZ` they are `shift`, which is exact at any count. On a fixed-size type, `LSHIFT` loses the bits shifted out and throws nothing. `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, and one that a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. At a negative power, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws `DivisionByZero`, and any other base throws `IntegerOverflow`. The library follows the same power rule under walk; the compiled path's own library does not (F-263). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-98` (the conversions and the shifts) and `:562-574` (the power); `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-268` (`GCD` and `LCM`).
=== F-173
- F-173 **The specification's type-inference chapter states the rule that the compiled checker builds: the declaration is chosen first, then its static arguments are inferred.** It states P-46, P-48 and P-49. A type parameter that a parameter's declared type mentions inside another type, as `List[\T\]` mentions `T`, is fixed by the argument at that position. One that is the whole declared type of one or more parameters, as `T` is of `x: T`, and that nothing else fixes, takes the narrowest type, within its bounds, that every one of those arguments has or converts into: `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32`. Where there is none, and no numeral settles the tie, it takes its bound, narrowed by what the call's expected type requires of the return type (P-48). So does a type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes. Inference never gives a type parameter `BottomType`. The compiled path departs from the chapter in these ways, among others. Its prelude lacks the coercion of `NN32` into `ZZ64`, so a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` instantiate a type parameter at `ZZ`, not `ZZ64`; no callout names this (row 442, `compiler_tests/XXXInferPromoteNN32`). The callouts at `Specification/basic/inference.tex:285-347` and `:448-512` also give walk's departures, such as the return type `BottomType` that walk gives a function expression that declares none (row 587). Plain tests gate the rule for a type parameter that is a parameter's whole type, at its bound where no argument type is narrowest, on both paths: `compiler_tests/InferLone*` and `tests/InferLone*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md` (the bound rule); `Specification/basic/inference.tex:45-125` (the chapter's rule).
=== F-174
- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration over all its instances within its bounds.** It states P-45 and P-42. The section "Declarations with Static Parameters" states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet. It gives one more restriction as the compiled path's, not the language's. Where one generic declaration is more specific than another with as many static parameters, the two must declare them of the same kinds, position by position. Also, the more specific one's return type must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are matched by position, so the checker refuses an override whose return type reorders its static parameters (row 398, fixed). The section "Principles of Overloading" forbids overloading a functional whose single parameter's type is a type parameter with the bound `Any` written, as `T extends Any`. A type parameter with no `extends` clause, whose bound is also `Any`, is exempt. Both paths refuse such an overload: the checker in `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny`, and walk since row 534's fix. Neither path runs every set that the rules allow. Appendix I's entry "Overloading with static parameters" names the sets that each path fails. In row 1048, the checker refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`. In row 537, the code generator fails on two generic declarations whose bounds differ. In row 539, walk refuses at load the 2019 paper's valid set over an array list and a list. In rows 779 and 780, walk fails on two generic functional methods one of whose declared domains lies inside the other's: in a trait or object without static parameters it refuses them at load, and in a trait with static parameters it stops with an error when an extending object's first instance is made. Detail: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:134-150` and `:531-674`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
=== F-175
- F-175 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values in every passage.** It builds P-60. Appendix I's entry "Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values" records the change. A call whose argument's static type stands between two closed traits runs the declaration that covers its value. Where its declarations have no static parameters, its type is the intersection of its most specific declarations' return types. Appendix I names three places where the compiled path departs. The checker checks a `comprises` clause at the closed trait's immediate subtypes only (row 487). The checker refuses the Meet Rule's example for closed traits when its declarations have static parameters (row 546). The checker's verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Detail: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3486-3681`, with the rows at `:1677` and `:3752-3755`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 8 and 9.
=== F-176
- F-176 **The specification allows arithmetic in a size, and two size arguments are identical when they are written alike once each operation whose operands are numerals is replaced by its value.** It states P-55. By the grammar, a size is a numeral, a name, a sum, a difference, a product, a power to a numeral or a name, or a bracketed size. So `2 3` and `6` are identical, but `s0 s1` and `s1 s0` are not. Two types are identical when they have the same name and identical static arguments, sizes compared this way. Two sizes are known to differ when they are two different numerals. A static parameter, or a size in which one occurs, is not known to differ from a numeral, since an instance may make them equal. F-146 gives the compiled checker, and F-222 walk's arithmetic. When walk infers a size parameter from a call's argument type, it matches a numeral and binds a name, and solves no size written as an operation: read in `IntNat.unifyStaticArg` (`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java:126-147`), and observed in row 767. Source: `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:49-62`; `Specification/appendices/grammars/concrete-syntax.tex:533-547` (`IntExpr`).
=== F-223
- F-223 **The specification's No Duplicates Rule is the papers' non-strict rule, and the compiled checker applies it, to functional methods wherever their `self` parameters stand, abstract ones included.** Two declarations of one name may not each be applicable to every call to which the other is, as in the type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 (P-26). The checker refuses such a pair, two functional methods at different `self` positions and an abstract functional method beside a concrete one among them: "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first. It checks symbolic operators too (F-281): `opr ||(self, y: S)` beside `opr ||(x: S, self)` in a trait `S` is refused, 'There are multiple declarations of || with the same parameter type: (S)'. Walk refuses at load such a pair of two generic declarations whose parameter types mention their static parameters, as `dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\])`; it refuses too a generic declaration beside one whose parameter types are its bounds, a plain one or a generic one whose parameter types mention none of its static parameters, 'fails because their parameter lists have the same types'. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRule`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions`, the symbolic operator's case by `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator`, walk's refusal by `tests/NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, and those two refusals by `tests/GenericBesidePlainSameDomain` and `GenericBesideGenericSameDomain`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md` section 4, its `SKEPTIC.md` section 2, `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8, and `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.
=== F-271
- F-271 **The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives P-48's instance rule, and its soundness proof does not cover the library's F-bounded functions, such as `SUM` and `BIG MAX`.** By P-48's rule, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes the intersection of its upper bounds. The paper is later than both the specification and the team's restart (F-166). Its calculus does not let a method type parameter occur in an upper bound, so F-bounded method parameters are outside it. It also leaves out top-level functions and functional methods, among other limits. `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` checks the curator's decisions against the paper. Detail: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md` sections 6 and 8.
=== F-272
- F-272 **The coercion example of the specification's "Coercion Resolution", over its own traits `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ128`, declares the exclusions that the chapter's definitions need: `ZZ32 excludes { ZZ64, ZZ128 }` and `ZZ64 excludes { ZZ128 }`.** A type `T` rejects `U` when every type that coerces to `T` excludes `U`. `T` is no less specific than `U` when it is a subtype of `U`, or excludes, coerces to and rejects it. So the choice of the more specific declaration depends on the exclusions. In the rung's probe, with the traits renamed `S32`, `S64` and `S128`, since the first two names are the library's, the revised example ran on both paths: `f(S32Of)`, on an `S32` value, chose `f` on `S64` and gave 1. No gated test runs the printed example. Row 394, fixed, names `tests/CoercionMostSpecificRungC.fss`, a walk test of the choice of the more specific coercion over three traits of the example's shape, each of which excludes both others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 4, decision 6; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:558-574` (the definitions) and `:641` onward (the example).
=== F-273
- F-273 **The specification gives the run-time instance of a generic declaration that dispatch reaches, and that the static call did not select, by the POPL 2019 paper's rule.** It builds P-48. A declaration that the static call selected runs at the instance inferred for the call (F-173). Where an argument's value fixes a type parameter, as a value of `Tag[\X\]` fixes `X`, the rule and both paths agree. Where a type parameter is a parameter's whole type, the argument's run-time type only bounds it from below. The rule then gives it its declared bound, narrowed by what the call's static type requires of the return type. The dispatch paragraph's callout says that both paths take the argument's run-time type there instead. Walk always will, since it has no static types (P-48). The compiled path does so because its dispatcher is not given the call's static type (row 538, the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed`). The callout also says that the compiled path does not yet run the paragraph's second example, a generic declaration beside a plain one, reached through an argument of static type `Any` (row 496). Detail: `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:312-349`, in the chapter "Overloading and Multiple Dispatch"; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 5 and 6.
=== F-300
- F-300 **The type group's POPL 2019 paper, its technical report and the report's LaTeX sources are in `Papers/Variance/`.** The paper, Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance" (POPL 2019, doi:10.1145/3290324), is `3290324-popl19w.pdf`, under the CC BY-NC 4.0 licence that its first page prints. The technical report, the paper extended with the formalization in its appendices, is `3290324-popl19-TR.pdf`; the report and its sources (`paper.tex` and the files it reads) are included with Sukyoung Ryu's permission, and the report prints no licence of its own. ACM's `acmart.cls` and `ACM-Reference-Format.bst` there carry ACM's own terms. The working notes on the paper, its full text and its talk's transcript stay in `research/extracts/`. Read in the tree. Detail: `Papers/Variance/README.md`, "Permission and licence".
=== F-319
- F-319 **A comparison at a NaN or at 0/0 answers `false`, on the specification's word too.** It builds P-159. The overview of operators says that `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` return `false` at a floating-point NaN and at the rational 0/0, that `CMP` returns `Unordered` at a NaN, and that -1/0 and 1/0 are ordered below and above every finite rational (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, "Comparisons Operators"; Appendix I, "A comparison at a NaN or at the rational indefinite"); walk answers so, and the compiled path at a NaN (its library has no `CMP` on floats); nothing raises `FloatingComparisonError` or `RationalComparisonError`, which stay declared. Walk departs at 0/0 against itself, `true` for `=`, `<=` and `>=` and `EqualTo` for `CMP` (row 440). The team's later restart, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Operators/operator-overview.tick`, still says both comparisons raise: the rung that revised `Specification/` left it as the team wrote it, outside its files (climb batch 26's rung S). Test: `tests/ComparisonAtNaNWalk`, and the NaN asserts of `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyFloatCompiled` and `NativeHelperFamilyRR32Compiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-nan-comparison/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2 and 7.
=== F-345
- F-345 **The specification states, in the revision form, the static numerals (P-174, P-176) and P-171's string literals.** The literals chapter gives a numeral a numeral type that exists only at compile time, `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` below a `Numeral` without static parameters, the four numbers its static arguments, naturals of any size, and every number type's coercion generic over the four numbers, each converted where it stands, and folded, one value per place. It also gives the conversion where a place fixes a type and the default elsewhere; a program's type receiving a numeral as written, its minus on the coercion's result, any other static expression through its coercion from the default's type; a `where` clause over the four numbers refusing statically; and the numeral types written only as parameter types (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:98-302`). The constant chapter gives the fold, converted from its exact value at a library type (`constant.tex:80-126`). The numbers chapter gives the coercions, with no `=` pairs and no `asFloat` on a numeral type (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:47-71`). The binary chapter's numeral declarations are expressible now and left out. Appendix I gives `revival-numerals`, `revival-numeral-numbers` and `revival-string-literals` (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), whose Effects name each departure of the two implementations with its row. Test: the specification's build (`ant genSource`, `ant tex`), 0 warnings by the skill's grep. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals-spec/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
=== F-359
- F-359 **The prelude's built-in number types were objects when first written, and became traits to nest them and to hold the literal objects; both reasons are gone from both libraries.** `object ZZ32 extends Number`, with `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64`, is of 2009-03-03 (`b2880c05c2`, Flood), the shape of the interpreter's library. They became traits on 2009-03-30 (`76c267f987`, Maessen: `trait ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, `object IntLiteral extends ZZ32`), and stayed traits when Chase flattened the tower (`6896886fbc`, 2009-08-31); the later built-in types followed the pattern. Chase's paper on the mapping calls the hand-written classes that carry these traits at run time, such as `FZZ32`, special cases "for the time being" (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:91-92`), and gives as the rule that a trait is an interface and an object a final class. His plan for unboxing (`compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`) is written over objects and `comprises` clauses and has no case for an open trait. So the trait form of a type that a hand-written class carries is later in date for every type, and the sources do not settle whether it is a decision of the team's in the sense of P-26. Read in the history and the texts. Command: `git log --full-history --reverse -S'object ZZ32' a874948ac -- ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`. Detail: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "What the team's texts say, by provenance".
=== F-371
- F-371 **The team's texts describe no inference of the types that a declaration leaves out, beyond copying them from the exported api; for a method's types taken from the declaration that it implements, the Working Draft holds one sentence and two printed examples, and no rule.** The examples are `catalyze(reaction)` in trait `Enzyme`, with the sentence that it implements `Catalyst`'s abstract method, and `append(xs)` in object `Cons`. The Working Draft's chapter on whole-program inference is a heading and notes (F-169, on static-argument inference, reads the same chapter). The 2012 restart's chapter is a heading, and the type group's papers, the POPL 2019 paper among them, infer only a call's type arguments and write every parameter type. So row 405's gap, and a parameter whose type only its uses could give, as in the overview's `f(x) = x^2 + sin x - cos 2 x`, have no design of the team to build: a citation for them cites examples, not a rule. Evidence: read in the specification, the restart and `Papers/`; not searched: the 2012 patents, the printed versions 1.0 alpha and beta, and an email of 2007 that the draft's note cites. Detail: `explorations/reviews/omitted-types-intent-2026-11-16.md`, "What the designers' texts and code say" and "The team's own examples that leave types out".
